'''''Closterium''''' is a [[genus (biology)|genus]] of desmid, a group of [[charophyte]] [[green algae]].<ref>See the [[National Center for Biotechnology Information|NCBI]] [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Taxonomy/Browser/wwwtax.cgi?mode=Info&id=34145 webpage on Closterium]. Data extracted from the {{cite web | url=https://ftp.ncbi.nih.gov/pub/taxonomy/ | title=NCBI taxonomy resources | publisher=[[National Center for Biotechnology Information]] | access-date=2007-03-19}}</ref> It is placed in the family [[Closteriaceae]].<ref name=Bicudo_and_Menezes2006/> Species of ''Closterium'' are a common component of freshwater [[microalgae]] flora worldwide.<ref name=Bellinger_and_Sigee/>

== Description ==
''Closterium'' is a diverse genus consisting of solitary cells, each made of two identical halves called semicells. Usually they are microscopic, but the largest can become easily visible to the naked eye. Cells are many times longer than broad, and are variously elongate to lunate (crescent-shaped). The poles are rounded, truncated, or pointed. The surface of the cell may be smooth or decorated with various features, such as striations or punctae. The cell wall is transparent, but with age it may become dark brown due to accumulated [[iron]] and [[manganese]] compounds.<ref name=Bicudo_and_Menezes2006>{{cite book | title= Gêneros de Algas de Águas Continentais do Brasil: chave para identificação e descrições | edition=2 | year=2006 | first1=Carlos E. M. |last1=Bicudo | first2=Mariângela | last2= Menezes | publisher= RiMa Editora | pages=508 | isbn= 857656064X }}</ref> The [[cell nucleus]] is located in the middle of the cell. Each semicell contains a single axial [[chloroplast]] dotted with several [[pyrenoid]]s.<ref name=Hall2014>{{cite book |editor-first1=John D.|editor-last1=Wehr|editor-first2=Robert G.|editor-last2=Sheath|editor-first3=J. Patrick|editor-last3=Kociolek |date= 2014 |edition=2 |title= Freshwater Algae of North America: Ecology and Classification |last1= Hall|first1=John D.| last2=McCourt |first2=Richard M. |chapter= Chapter 9. Conjugating Green Algae Including Desmids |url= |location= |publisher= Elsevier Inc. |page= |isbn=978-0-12-385876-4 }}</ref>

At either end of the cell, there is a generally a polar [[vacuole]]. The vacuoles often contain conspicuous [[barium sulfate]] crystals.<ref name=Hall2014/>

== Taxonomy ==
''Closterium regulare'' was first described from Lower Normandy by Brebisson.<ref name="undefined">Carter, C.F. and Williamson, D.B. (2008) A rediscovered UK desmid: ''Closterium regulare'' Breb ''The Phycologist.'' Autumn 2008 No.75:24</ref> The name comes from the Greek word ''klosterion'', meaning a small [[spindle (textiles)|spindle]].<ref name=CarolinaLucidKey>{{cite web|url=https://fmp.conncoll.edu/Silicasecchidisk/LucidKeys3.5/Keys_v3.5/Carolina35_Key/Media/Html/Closterium_Main.html|title=Closterium|first1= Hannah|last1= Shayler|first2=Peter A.|last2=Siver|work=Carolina Lucid Key to Freshwater Algae|publisher=Connecticut College | date=2004 |access-date=2024-11-28 }}</ref>

== Reproduction ==
'''Asexual:''' binary fission from a partitioned parent cell.

'''Sexual:''' Conjugation to form a hypnozygote.

The ''Closterium peracerosum-strigosum-littorale (C. psl)'' complex is a [[unicellular organism|unicellular]], [[isogamy|isogamous]] [[Charophyceae|charophycea]]n [[Algae|alga]] cells that is the closest unicellular relative to land plants.  These algae are capable of forming two types of dormant [[Ploidy#Diploid|diploid]] [[zygospore]]s.  Some populations form zygospores within single [[Clone (cell biology)|clone]]s of cells ([[Homothallism|homothallic]]), whereas others form zygospores between different clones of cells ([[heterothallic]]).  The heterothallic strains have two [[mating type]]s, mt(-) and mt(+).  When cells of opposite mating types are mixed in a nitrogen-deficient mating medium, mt(-) and mt(+) cells pair with each other and release protoplasts. This release is then followed by protoplast fusion (conjugation) leading to formation of a diploid zygospore.  Sex [[pheromone]]s termed protoplast-release inducing proteins produced by mt(-) and mt(+) cells facilitate this process.<ref name="pmid24197184">{{cite journal |vauthors=Sekimoto H, Satoh S, Fujii T |title=Biochemical and physiological properties of a protein inducing protoplast release during conjugation in theClosterium peracerosum-strigosum-littorale complex |journal=Planta |volume=182 |issue=3 |pages=348–54 |year=1990 |pmid=24197184 |doi=10.1007/BF02411384 |s2cid=1999634 }}</ref>

A homothallic strain of Closterium forms selfing zygospores via the conjugation of two sister gametangial cells derived from one vegetative cell.<ref name="pmid20656896">{{cite journal |vauthors=Tsuchikane Y, Kokubun Y, Sekimoto H |title=Characterization and molecular cloning of conjugation-regulating sex pheromones in homothallic Closterium |journal=Plant Cell Physiol. |volume=51 |issue=9 |pages=1515–23 |year=2010 |pmid=20656896 |doi=10.1093/pcp/pcq110 |doi-access=free }}</ref>   Conjugation in the homothallic strain occurs mainly at low cell density and is regulated by an [[Homology (biology)#Orthology|ortholog]] of a heterothallic sex-specific pheromone.

Although self-fertilization employs [[meiosis]], it produces minimal genetic variability. [[Homothallism]] is thus a form of sex that is unlikely to be adaptively maintained by a benefit related to producing variability. However, homothallic meiosis may be maintained in ''Closterium peracerosum'' as an adaptation for surviving under stressful conditions such as growth in nitrogen depleted media at low cell density.  A proposed adaptive benefit of meiosis is the promotion of [[homologous recombination]]al repair of [[DNA damage (naturally occurring)|DNA damages]] that can be caused by a stressful environment <ref name="pmid27605505">{{cite journal |vauthors=Mirzaghaderi G, Hörandl E |title=The evolution of meiotic sex and its alternatives |journal=Proc. Biol. Sci. |volume=283 |issue=1838 |year=2016 |pmid=27605505 |pmc=5031655 |doi=10.1098/rspb.2016.1221 }}</ref>

==Habitats==
Like other desmids, ''Closterium'' is found in [[freshwater]] habitats. ''Closterium'' is usually attached to sediments or aquatic plants, but may sometimes be [[planktonic]], i.e. free-floating in the water column, or found in wet soils.<ref name=Hall2014/> Most species prefer oligotrophic and slightly acidic waters, but a few species (for example ''[[Closterium aciculare]]'') prefer eutrophic, slightly alkaline lakes.<ref name=Bellinger_and_Sigee>{{cite book | isbn=978-1-118-91716-9 | title=Freshwater Algae: Identification, Enumeration and Use as Bioindicators | edition=2nd | last1=Bellinger | first1=Edward G. | last2=Sigee | first2=David C. | date=23 February 2015 | publisher=Wiley }}</ref>
